name: Phase-based trauma treatment and sequencing decisions
purpose: A guide to deciding when, and whether, to add a stabilization phase before trauma-focused therapy. The classic phase-oriented model has three stages: safety and stabilization, processing of trauma memories, and reintegration into daily life. Current guidelines recommend trauma-focused therapies as first-line care for post-traumatic stress, and trials show that many people, including those with childhood or repeated trauma, benefit without a long, mandatory stabilization phase. Sequencing is therefore a case-by-case clinical decision with a review date, not a default waiting period.
whenToUse: When planning treatment for post-traumatic stress, especially after repeated or early-life trauma.
When the ICD-11 pattern of complex PTSD may apply: post-traumatic stress plus lasting problems with emotion regulation, self-concept and relationships.
When someone has been in stabilization work for a long time and trauma-focused therapy has not started.
When current safety, dissociation or self-harm raise the question of what to do first.

structure.label: Phase 1: Safety and stabilization
structure.prompt: Establish current safety, a working alliance, psychoeducation and enough emotion-regulation and grounding skills to take part in therapy. Keep this phase focused and time-limited, with a planned review.
examples: Agree on a grounding plan for sessions
Link with housing or legal help if the person is still in danger

structure.label: Phase 2: Processing trauma memories
structure.prompt: A recommended trauma-focused therapy, chosen with the person and delivered by a trained clinician. Skills from phase 1 continue alongside.
examples: Weekly sessions of a chosen protocol with between-session practice

structure.label: Phase 3: Reintegration
structure.prompt: Rebuilding relationships, roles, meaning and plans for the future, and preparing for setbacks.

structure.label: What the evidence says about sequencing
structure.prompt: Expert consensus once favored a stabilization phase for complex presentations. Later reviews found little evidence that a mandatory phase improves outcomes, and trials of trauma-focused therapies included many people with complex histories who did well. Delaying processing can itself cause harm by prolonging symptoms.

structure.label: When a brief focus on safety first may make sense
structure.prompt: Ongoing danger (for example a current abusive relationship), a current suicidal crisis or frequent self-harm, dissociation so severe the person cannot stay present in sessions, unmanaged withdrawal or intoxication, or acute psychosis or mania. Even then, set a review date and start trauma-focused work as soon as the barrier is addressed.
examples: Safety plan and lethal-means counseling in place before memory work
Dissociation screening and grounding practice first

structure.label: Complex PTSD (ICD-11)
structure.prompt: ICD-11 describes complex PTSD as post-traumatic stress together with lasting disturbances in self-organization: difficulty regulating emotions, a persistent negative view of oneself with shame or guilt, and difficulty feeling close to others. Treatment usually uses the same trauma-focused therapies, sometimes with more sessions and added skills work.

steps: Assess current safety, ongoing threat, self-harm, dissociation and substance use before choosing a start point; do not decide risk with a score.
Explain the treatment options and the evidence in plain words, including that stabilization is not always needed first.
If you sequence, name the specific barrier, the skills or changes that would address it, and a review date (for example in four to six sessions).
Choose a recommended trauma-focused therapy that fits the person's preferences and that you or a referral partner are trained to deliver.
Keep grounding and emotion-regulation skills available during processing, and plan for reintegration and relapse prevention.
collaborativeTips: Let the person decide how much of their story to tell during assessment; details can wait for the processing phase.
Make the plan predictable: what each phase involves, how long, and how you will both know it is time to move on.
cautions: Do not use memory-recovery techniques or suggest that someone has hidden trauma memories; work only with what the person remembers and reports.
Do not offer routine single-session psychological debriefing straight after a traumatic event; guidelines advise against it.
Trauma-focused protocols require formal training; refer when the needed therapy is outside your competence.
Severe dissociation calls for specialist assessment; this page does not cover dissociative presentations in depth.

A formulation never scores, grades or decides risk. If thoughts of suicide, self-harm or harm to others come up, pause the formulation and follow your own assessment and local protocol; in the US the 988 Lifeline is available by call or text, elsewhere use the local emergency number or findahelpline.com.
dsmPointer: See DSM-5-TR: Trauma- and Stressor-Related Disorders (Posttraumatic Stress Disorder). ICD-10-CM has no separate code for complex PTSD.
trainingRequired: Trained clinicians only for the trauma-focused protocols (for example prolonged exposure, cognitive processing therapy, cognitive therapy for PTSD, EMDR, narrative exposure therapy and written exposure therapy). Each has its own training route.
